The intermediate branch joins (10 V,1 A) to (4 V,4 A). The upper branch starts at (4 V,4 A) and its extension passes through the origin. Holding voltage Uh=4.00 V and threshold Uth=10.0 V. The supplied circuits use ideal components. All numerical evaluations below use R=3.00 Ω, E=15.0 V, L=1.00 μH for part A and C=1.00 μF for parts B and C. Switching between branches is instantaneous.

statement.text:
Nonlinear Dynamics in Electric Circuits
A bistable element X has the piecewise-linear I to U characteristic in the figure. The lower branch goes from (0 V,0 A) to (10 V,1 A). The intermediate branch joins (10 V,1 A) to (4 V,4 A). The upper branch starts at (4 V,4 A) and its extension passes through the origin. Holding voltage Uh=4.00 V and threshold Uth=10.0 V. The supplied circuits use ideal components. All numerical evaluations below use R=3.00 Ω, E=15.0 V, L=1.00 μH for part A and C=1.00 μF for parts B and C. Switching between branches is instantaneous.

a1. Characteristic parameters
Find Roff, Ron, Rint and I0 in the intermediate-branch equation \(I=I_0-U/R_{int}\).
a2. Number of stationary states

Connect E, R, L and X in series. Show graphically how stationary states are found. How many are possible as E varies for R=3 Ω and R=1 Ω?
a3. Series operating point
For R=3 Ω and E=15 V calculate stationary I and U.
a4. Inductive stability
Determine and justify the stability of the part A3 stationary state.
b1. Capacitive limit cycle

Now remove L and connect C in parallel with X, fed by E through R. Draw the closed oscillation cycle on the I to U diagram, with directions and reasons for the jumps.
b2. Oscillation period
Derive the voltage evolution on each branch, its dwell time and total period.
b3. Power estimate
Estimate the mean power dissipated in X to order of magnitude and explain the estimate.
b4. Transmitter antenna
The oscillation feeds an antenna with a free end. Find its optimal length s below 1 km using c=3.00×10^8 m/s.
c1. Neuristor pulse sketches

Initially the capacitive circuit is stationary at Etilde=12.0 V. At t0 increase the supply to 15.0 V for duration τ<T, then return to 12.0 V. Sketch IX(t) for τ below and above a critical duration, and explain the difference.
c2. Critical pulse duration
Derive and evaluate the duration needed to first reach Uth.
c3. Firing decision
For τ=1.00 μs, does the circuit act as a neuristor? Justify.

children.text: The lower and upper slopes give \(R_{off}=10.0\,\Omega\), \(R_{on}=1.00\,\Omega\). The middle slope is −0.5 A/V, so \(R_{int}=2.00\,\Omega\), \(I_0=6.00\,\mathrm A\).

At a stationary state \(E=RI+U\). Intersections of \(I=(E-U)/R\) with the characteristic give the states. For R=3 Ω there is exactly one. For R=1 Ω there may be one, two at a corner, or three. The two-state corner cases must not be omitted.
The physical intersection lies on the intermediate branch. \(I=(E-R_{int}I_0)/(R-R_{int})=3.00\,\mathrm A\), and \(U=R_{int}(I_0-I)=6.00\,\mathrm V\).
Kirchhoff's law gives \(L\dot I=E-R_{int}I_0-(R-R_{int})I\). A perturbation obeys \(L\delta\dot I=-(R-R_{int})\delta I\). Because R−Rint=1 Ω>0 the state is stable, with decay time L/(R−Rint)=1 μs.

Voltage is continuous across the capacitor, so jumps are vertical. On the off branch voltage increases from Uh to Uth, jumps to the on branch at Uth, decreases to Uh, then jumps to the off branch. The middle-branch stationary state is unstable in this capacitive circuit. The branch equilibria lie outside the allowed branch intervals, so motion continues to each corner.

For branch resistance r, \(C\dot U=(E-U)/R-U/r\). Define \(U_r=Er/(R+r)\), \(t_r=CRr/(R+r)\). Then \(U(t)=U_r+[U(0)-U_r]e^{-t/t_r}\). Thus \[t_{on}=t_{R_{on}}\ln\frac{U_{th}-U_{on}}{U_h-U_{on}}=2.41\,\mu s,\quad t_{off}=t_{R_{off}}\ln\frac{U_{off}-U_h}{U_{off}-U_{th}}=3.71\,\mu s.\] Their sum is T=6.12 μs.

The on branch dominates. Estimating U by (Uh+Uth)/2 gives \(\overline P\sim[(U_h+U_{th})/2]^2t_{on}/(R_{on}T)\simeq19\,\mathrm W\). The source accepts justified estimates between 5 and 50 W. This is an estimate rather than an exact integral.
For the fundamental quarter-wave mode, \(s=cT/4=459\,\mathrm m\). Other odd quarter-wave lengths exceed 1 km.

Initially \(\widetilde U=12R_{off}/(R+R_{off})=9.23\,\mathrm V\). A short pulse raises U on the off branch but does not reach Uth, so current returns smoothly from above to its original value. A longer pulse reaches Uth, jumps to the on branch, decays there and jumps back at Uh. It then approaches the original off-branch state from below. The firing pulse is an all-or-nothing large excursion.
Using the off-branch exponential, \[\tau_{crit}=\frac{CRR_{off}}{R+R_{off}}\ln\frac{U_{off}-\widetilde U}{U_{off}-U_{th}}=0.936\,\mu s.\]
Yes. Since 1.00 μs exceeds 0.936 μs, the threshold is crossed and one large current excursion occurs before the original stationary state is recovered.

solution.text:
Nonlinear Dynamics in Electric Circuits
a1. Characteristic parameters
The lower and upper slopes give \(R_{off}=10.0\,\Omega\), \(R_{on}=1.00\,\Omega\). The middle slope is −0.5 A/V, so \(R_{int}=2.00\,\Omega\), \(I_0=6.00\,\mathrm A\).
a2. Number of stationary states
At a stationary state \(E=RI+U\). Intersections of \(I=(E-U)/R\) with the characteristic give the states. For R=3 Ω there is exactly one. For R=1 Ω there may be one, two at a corner, or three. The two-state corner cases must not be omitted.
a3. Series operating point
The physical intersection lies on the intermediate branch. \(I=(E-R_{int}I_0)/(R-R_{int})=3.00\,\mathrm A\), and \(U=R_{int}(I_0-I)=6.00\,\mathrm V\).
a4. Inductive stability
Kirchhoff's law gives \(L\dot I=E-R_{int}I_0-(R-R_{int})I\). A perturbation obeys \(L\delta\dot I=-(R-R_{int})\delta I\). Because R−Rint=1 Ω>0 the state is stable, with decay time L/(R−Rint)=1 μs.
b1. Capacitive limit cycle
Voltage is continuous across the capacitor, so jumps are vertical. On the off branch voltage increases from Uh to Uth, jumps to the on branch at Uth, decreases to Uh, then jumps to the off branch. The middle-branch stationary state is unstable in this capacitive circuit. The branch equilibria lie outside the allowed branch intervals, so motion continues to each corner.
b2. Oscillation period
For branch resistance r, \(C\dot U=(E-U)/R-U/r\). Define \(U_r=Er/(R+r)\), \(t_r=CRr/(R+r)\). Then \(U(t)=U_r+[U(0)-U_r]e^{-t/t_r}\). Thus \[t_{on}=t_{R_{on}}\ln\frac{U_{th}-U_{on}}{U_h-U_{on}}=2.41\,\mu s,\quad t_{off}=t_{R_{off}}\ln\frac{U_{off}-U_h}{U_{off}-U_{th}}=3.71\,\mu s.\] Their sum is T=6.12 μs.
b3. Power estimate
The on branch dominates. Estimating U by (Uh+Uth)/2 gives \(\overline P\sim[(U_h+U_{th})/2]^2t_{on}/(R_{on}T)\simeq19\,\mathrm W\). The source accepts justified estimates between 5 and 50 W. This is an estimate rather than an exact integral.
b4. Transmitter antenna
For the fundamental quarter-wave mode, \(s=cT/4=459\,\mathrm m\). Other odd quarter-wave lengths exceed 1 km.
c1. Neuristor pulse sketches
Initially \(\widetilde U=12R_{off}/(R+R_{off})=9.23\,\mathrm V\). A short pulse raises U on the off branch but does not reach Uth, so current returns smoothly from above to its original value. A longer pulse reaches Uth, jumps to the on branch, decays there and jumps back at Uh. It then approaches the original off-branch state from below. The firing pulse is an all-or-nothing large excursion.
c2. Critical pulse duration
Using the off-branch exponential, \[\tau_{crit}=\frac{CRR_{off}}{R+R_{off}}\ln\frac{U_{off}-\widetilde U}{U_{off}-U_{th}}=0.936\,\mu s.\]
c3. Firing decision
Yes. Since 1.00 μs exceeds 0.936 μs, the threshold is crossed and one large current excursion occurs before the original stationary state is recovered.
